def: Green chemistry is the design of chemical products and processes that reduce or eliminate the use and generation of hazardous substances, protecting the environment.
points: Prevent waste rather than treat or clean it up after it is formed.
Design safer chemicals and products that have little or no toxicity.
Use renewable raw materials/feedstock instead of depleting ones wherever possible.
Maximise atom economy so most reactant atoms end up in the final product.
Use catalysts (reusable) instead of stoichiometric reagents to reduce waste and energy use.
Design processes for energy efficiency, carried out at room temperature and pressure where possible.
formula: No chemical formula - 12 principles framework; key concept: Atom Economy% = (mass of desired product / total mass of reactants) x 100

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["Green Chemistry Principles"] --> B["Prevent waste"]
  A --> C["Safer chemicals"]
  A --> D["Renewable feedstock"]
  A --> E["Atom economy and catalysts"]
  A --> F["Energy efficient process"]

example: Using hydrogen peroxide (gives only water as by-product) instead of chlorine-based bleach is a green chemistry choice.
tip: List 4-5 principles with a one-line explanation each - full marks need variety, not depth.

def: Green synthesis means preparing chemical products using methods that are safer, use less hazardous solvents/reagents, and produce less waste than conventional methods.
points: Synthesis of adipic acid: traditional method used nitric acid oxidation (releases nitrous oxide, a pollutant); green method uses hydrogen peroxide as oxidant with a catalyst, giving only water as by-product.
Synthesis of urethane: traditionally made using toxic phosgene gas; green process avoids toxic intermediates.
Use of microwave and ultrasound-assisted reactions to speed up synthesis with less solvent and energy.
Use of water or supercritical CO2 as green solvents instead of volatile organic solvents.
Dry media reactions (solid-state, solvent-free reactions) reduce solvent waste.
formula: No single formula - concept example: traditional adipic acid synthesis releases N2O; green method uses H2O2 giving only H2O as by-product

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Traditional synthesis"] --> B["Uses toxic reagent or solvent"]
  B --> C["Generates harmful by products"]
  D["Green synthesis"] --> E["Uses safer reagent like H2O2"]
  E --> F["Gives only water as by product"]

example: Green synthesis of adipic acid using H2O2 and a catalyst avoids the nitrous oxide pollution of the older nitric acid method.
tip: The adipic acid example is the most commonly asked green synthesis case - learn it with both old and new method.

def: Atom economy is a measure of how much of the reactant atoms are incorporated into the desired final product of a chemical reaction, expressed as a percentage.
points: It compares the molar mass of the desired product to the sum of molar masses of all reactants.
Higher atom economy means less waste is produced - a key goal of green chemistry.
Addition reactions generally have 100% atom economy since no atoms are lost.
Substitution and elimination reactions often have lower atom economy as some atoms leave as by-products.
Choosing reaction routes with higher atom economy reduces raw material cost and environmental impact.
formula: Atom economy (%) = (molar mass of desired product / sum of molar masses of all reactants) x 100

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Reactants total mass"] --> B["Reaction occurs"]
  B --> C["Desired product mass"]
  B --> D["By products and waste mass"]
  C --> E["Atom economy percent calculated"]

example: For reaction A + B -> C + D, if molar mass of C (desired) is 80 and total reactant mass is 100, atom economy = (80/100) x 100 = 80%.
tip: Always show the formula and substitute numbers step by step - examiners award marks for the calculation method, not just the final answer.

def: Nanomaterials are materials having at least one dimension in the nanometre range (1 to 100 nm), classified by how many of their dimensions are in this nano range.
points: Zero-dimensional (0D): all three dimensions are in the nanoscale, e.g. nanoparticles, quantum dots.
One-dimensional (1D): one dimension is outside the nanoscale (length is large), e.g. nanowires, nanorods, nanotubes.
Two-dimensional (2D): two dimensions are outside the nanoscale (large surface), e.g. nanofilms, nanosheets, graphene.
Three-dimensional (3D) nanostructured materials: made of nanosized grains or particles arranged in bulk, e.g. nanocrystalline bulk materials.
Carbon-based nanomaterials: fullerenes, carbon nanotubes, graphene are important examples.
formula: Nanoscale range: 1 nm to 100 nm (1 nm = 10^-9 m)

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["Nanomaterials"] --> B["0D nanoparticles quantum dots"]
  A --> C["1D nanowires nanotubes"]
  A --> D["2D nanosheets graphene"]
  A --> E["3D nanocrystalline bulk"]

example: A carbon nanotube is a 1D nanomaterial because its diameter is in nanometres but its length can be much larger.
tip: State the size range (1-100 nm) first, then classify by dimension with one example each.

def: Nanomaterials show unique physical, chemical, electrical and mechanical properties that are different from the same substance in bulk form, mainly because of their very small size and large surface area.
points: Very high surface area to volume ratio compared to bulk material, making them more reactive and better catalysts.
Mechanical properties improve: nanomaterials are often much stronger and harder than the bulk form (e.g. carbon nanotubes are stronger than steel).
Optical properties change with particle size - e.g. gold nanoparticles appear red/purple instead of golden yellow.
Electrical and magnetic properties can differ greatly from bulk due to quantum effects at the nanoscale.
Melting point and other physical properties can be different (often lower) compared to the bulk material.
formula: Surface area to volume ratio increases greatly as particle size decreases (ratio proportional to 1/r)

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Bulk material"] --> B["Reduced to nanoscale size"]
  B --> C["Surface area to volume ratio increases"]
  C --> D["Changed optical electrical and mechanical properties"]

example: Bulk gold is yellow and unreactive, but gold nanoparticles appear red/purple and show high catalytic activity.
tip: Give at least three different property changes (optical, mechanical, surface area) with one example each for full marks.

def: Nanochemistry applications use the unique properties of nanomaterials in medicine, electronics, energy, and environmental fields to create better products and technologies.
points: Medicine: targeted drug delivery using nanoparticles, cancer treatment, and diagnostic imaging.
Electronics: nanomaterials used to make smaller, faster computer chips and transistors.
Energy: nanomaterials improve efficiency of solar cells and battery electrodes.
Environment: nanomaterials used for water purification (removing pollutants) and as catalysts to reduce emissions.
Textiles and coatings: nanoparticles (like silver nanoparticles) used for antibacterial and stain-resistant fabric.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["Nanochemistry applications"] --> B["Medicine drug delivery"]
  A --> C["Electronics smaller chips"]
  A --> D["Energy solar cells batteries"]
  A --> E["Environment water purification"]

example: Silver nanoparticles are coated on fabrics and bandages for their antibacterial action.
tip: List applications field-wise (medicine, electronics, energy, environment) with one example each - a safe way to cover a 5-mark answer.
